summary:
Selene Project is a free, browser-based app that lets anyone compare landing sites at the Moon's south pole and choose a date, then see where the Sun and the Earth sit relative to the horizon. In one view, mission planners, teachers and students can judge when a site has sunlight for solar power and when it has a direct line of sight to Earth for communication, including during lunar eclipses.
The app compares seven candidate sites (Haworth, Mons Mouton, Malapert Massif, Cabeus, Nobile, Connecting Ridge and the Shackleton rim). It covers every date from 2025 to 2040 with Sun and Earth positions computed from JPL's DE421 ephemeris and checked against JPL Horizons (largest difference 0.006°). It also adds terrain illumination results from LRO/LOLA and ice evidence from LCROSS and Chandrayaan-1's M3.
This matters because south-pole missions live or die by light and communication windows, and the existing tools are hard to use. Selene turns that data into an animated mission, a time-lapse from the surface, a first-person helmet view and a cooperative game in which a team builds a lunar base. That makes landing-site trade-offs easy to understand and fun to learn.
details:
Selene Project answers one planning question: at this landing site, on this date, will we have sunlight for power and Earth in view for communication? It is a single self-contained web page (HTML, CSS and JavaScript) that runs in any browser with no installation and no login, in English, Spanish, French and German.

What it does

Explorer mode (the planning tool):

  1. Compare sites. Seven south-pole candidates appear on a polar map and in a comparison table. Each shows Earth visibility (% of hours per year), the longest stretch without Earth, terrain sunlight where published studies exist, and ice evidence on a 0–3 scale.
  2. Pick any date from 2025 to 2040. A calendar frames every lunar eclipse (total, partial, penumbral) so planners can spot power risks at a glance.
  3. Fly the mission. An Apollo-style animation shows launch, staging, Earth orbit, trans-lunar injection, lunar orbit and descent. The lander waits in orbit until the user chooses a landing site.
  4. Stand on the surface. A 30-day time-lapse (one lunar day) shows the real path of the Sun and the Earth over the horizon. It includes Earth's phases, lighting and shadows, and eclipses where Earth covers the Sun. The live panel reports whether the Sun is up, whether Earth is in view, and the cumulative % of each.
  5. Look through the helmet. A first-person view with true angles lets users turn the camera to find the Sun and the Earth. At the pole they graze the horizon, which explains why terrain decides everything there.

Base Mission mode (learning by playing, solo or co-op for up to 4 players):

  1. Choose the base site and date, using real light and Earth percentages for the next 30 days.
  2. Load 13 modules into 4 ships (16 t each). Each ship flies a full cycle: launch, landing (automatic or a manual lander game with real lunar gravity, 1.62 m/s²), unloading on the Moon, and return to Earth for the next ship.
  3. Build the base on a top-down map following real siting logic: solar panels on the sunlit ridge, the antenna where Earth is visible, the ice drill on the rim of a permanently shadowed crater, everything within cable reach of the habitat. A drivable rover carries 3 crew or 2 crates.
  4. Turn ice into fuel by electrolysis (1 kg of water → 0.11 kg H₂ + 0.89 kg O₂). Power depends on the real Sun at that site and date, so lunar night and eclipses cut production unless batteries are installed.
  5. Keep the crew alive: life, water and food are replenished at the habitat, and drinking water also comes from the mined ice. Up to 4 players can join the same room with a 5-letter code, connecting browser-to-browser through PeerJS (WebRTC) with no accounts.

How it works

  • Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation for each site were computed every 6 hours for 2025–2040 from JPL's DE421 ephemeris, including the Moon's real orientation (librations). They were then verified against JPL Horizons, with a largest difference of 0.0003° in elevation and 0.006° in azimuth. The data is embedded in the page, so it works offline.
  • The lunar eclipses for 2025–2040 were computed from the same ephemeris and match NASA's eclipse catalogue in date and type.
  • Earth-visibility percentages were obtained directly from JPL Horizons for the year 2027.

Benefits

  • Planners: they can compare sites and dates in seconds instead of setting up ephemeris queries.
  • Teachers and students: they get a hands-on way to learn orbital geometry, energy and communication trade-offs, and in-situ resource use with real data.
  • The public: they can see why the next human landings are aimed at the lunar south pole.

Limitations

  • The Sun and Earth positions assume a smooth lunar sphere, as JPL Horizons does. Shadows from mountains and craters are only included through published LRO/LOLA results.
  • Production rates, cargo masses and build times in the game are simplified game values. Only the chemistry is real.
  • Co-op needs an internet connection; some school or company networks block the direct browser-to-browser (WebRTC) connections it uses.

Tools and languages

JavaScript (HTML5 Canvas), Python (NumPy, jplephem, the de421 package) for data processing, Playwright and FFmpeg for testing and video capture, and Kokoro TTS for the AI narration voice.
